- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model often overshoots; cap forecast at +3–5% above recent peak for next 3–5 days.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.33) and price is trending up, model underestimates; add 1–2% to forecast to account for sentiment-driven reversal.
- Model frequently underestimates true price in early horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead) when sentiment is neutral or slightly negative — adjust downward by 0.5–1.5% for short-term (1–3 day) forecasts.
- When sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and price is volatile, model tends to smooth out extremes — use a 3-day moving average of true values to anchor forecast midpoints.
- For long-term (10+ day) forecasts, model often fails to capture mean reversion — if price is above 30-day moving average, reduce forecast by 1–2% per week until reversion.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “0.00” (neutral or bearish), model tends to ignore sentiment and forecast based on pure price momentum — add 0.5–1.0% downward bias for such periods.
